nodes.label: The Sasanian Empire
nodes.full: The Persian state that governed the Arabian coast as provinces for four centuries — its garrisons, its Zoroastrian religion, its tax system and its Gulf trade route.
nodes.src: background — the Sasanian administrative geography of the Gulf (Potts 1990 vol. 2).

nodes.label: The Church of the East (Ctesiphon)
nodes.full: The wider church, seated at the Sasanian capital, whose synods the Gulf bishops attended and which organised the Gulf as the ecclesiastical province of Beth Qatraye.
nodes.src: background — the Synodicon Orientale.

nodes.label: Muhammad and the community at Medina
nodes.full: The new movement in the Hijaz whose letters and envoys reached al-Mundhir ibn Sawa in Bahrain and the Julanda brothers in Oman, bringing the Gulf into Islam by negotiation on the eve of this folio's close.
nodes.src: background — the Prophet's letters in the sira literature.

nodes.label: The Sasanian province system on the Arabian shore
nodes.full: After Ardashir's conquest the Sasanians governed the Arabian coast as provinces — Mishmahig on Bahrain, Hagar in the al-Hasa oasis, Mazun in Oman — each under a marzban (military governor) with Persian garrisons and settlers, an arrangement that held until the eve of Islam.
nodes.src: Sasanian administrative geography of the Gulf: the Šahrestānīhā ī Ērānšahr; al-Tabari on Persian governors of al-Bahrayn and Mazun; Potts (1990) vol. 2, ch. 7.

nodes.label: The Julanda dynasty rules Oman under Persian suzerainty
nodes.full: The Azdi house of Julanda held the Omani interior as kings, acknowledging Sasanian overlordship on the coast but running the mountains and oases themselves — the pattern of a strong interior and a foreign-influenced coast that recurs throughout Omani history.
nodes.src: Omani tradition preserved in al-Awtabi's 'Ansab al-Arab' and later Ibadi chronicles; the Julanda under Sasanian suzerainty (Wilkinson, 'The Imamate Tradition of Oman', 1987).

nodes.label: Al-Mundhir ibn Sawa accepts Islam in Bahrain
nodes.full: The Sasanian-appointed governor of Bahrain, al-Mundhir ibn Sawa of the Banu Tamim, received a letter from the Prophet Muhammad and converted, bringing eastern Arabia into the Muslim community by agreement rather than conquest.
nodes.src: The Prophet's letter to al-Mundhir ibn Sawa, preserved in Ibn Sa'd's 'Tabaqat' and al-Baladhuri's 'Futuh al-Buldan'; the jizya arrangement for the region's Zoroastrians, Jews and Christians.

nodes.label: Jayfar and Abd al-Julanda bring Oman into Islam
nodes.full: The brothers Jayfar and Abd, joint Julanda rulers of Oman, accepted Islam after receiving the Prophet's envoy Amr ibn al-As. Oman's peaceful entry into Islam, without a caliphal army, underlies its later insistence on governing itself.
nodes.src: al-Baladhuri, 'Futuh al-Buldan'; Omani sources (al-Awtabi); the mission of Amr ibn al-As to Oman, c.630.

nodes.label: Shapur II's campaign against the Arabs
nodes.full: Shapur II, called 'Dhu'l-Aktaf' ('he of the shoulders') for the way he punished captives, campaigned across eastern Arabia against tribes raiding into Iran, storming Hajar and deporting whole populations. It fixed Sasanian dominance over the Arabian shore for three centuries.
nodes.src: al-Tabari I.836–839 (Bosworth); the epithet Dhu'l-Aktaf. Cross-references the Sasanian Empire 224–484 folio.

nodes.label: The Lakhmids and the tribal buffer
nodes.full: The Sasanians managed the Arab tribes of the north-eastern peninsula through the Lakhmid (Naṣrid) kings of al-Hira, client rulers who policed the desert frontier, raided Byzantine clients and channelled Arabian trade. Eastern Arabia's tribes sat within this Persian-managed order until Khosrow II abolished the Lakhmid kingdom around 602.
nodes.src: The Lakhmids of al-Hira as a Sasanian buffer (Bosworth in the Cambridge History of Iran vol. 3; al-Tabari); the abolition of the kingdom c.602 and its role in loosening the desert frontier.

nodes.label: The last Byzantine–Sasanian war
nodes.full: The twenty-six-year war that ended with Heraclius's counter-offensive and the murder of Khosrow II left the Sasanian state financially and militarily broken. The Gulf province held on, but the empire that garrisoned it had spent itself — and within a decade a new power out of Arabia would sweep it away.
nodes.src: The 602–628 war (Howard-Johnston, 'Witnesses to a World Crisis', 2010); the fiscal and dynastic collapse of the late Sasanian state.

nodes.label: Sasanian military colonisation of the Gulf coast
nodes.full: The Sasanians planted Persian cavalry colonists (later the 'Asawira') and deported Arab tribes to develop the al-Hasa and Bahrain oases under the marzban's tax administration. The eastern Arabian coast became, in effect, an Iranian frontier province.
nodes.src: al-Tabari on Shapur II's deportations and the settlement of Persians; the Asawira who later defected to the Muslims at Basra (al-Baladhuri).

nodes.label: The Prophet's letter to al-Mundhir and the dhimma of Bahrain
nodes.full: The settlement with al-Mundhir ibn Sawa let the Zoroastrians, Jews and Christians of Bahrain keep their religion in return for the jizya tax. It is one of the earliest worked examples of the protected-minority arrangement that would govern non-Muslims across the caliphate.
nodes.src: Text in Ibn Sa'd, 'Tabaqat' I; al-Baladhuri, 'Futuh al-Buldan'; discussed by Morony, 'Iraq after the Muslim Conquest' (1984).

nodes.label: Sasanian fire worship on the Arabian shore
nodes.full: The Persian garrisons and settlers brought Zoroastrian fire ritual to the Gulf coast. Fire-holders and Sasanian religious imagery appear in the archaeology, and later Muslim writers remember 'Majus' (Zoroastrians) among the population of Bahrain and Oman.
nodes.src: Sasanian material from Gulf sites; the 'Majus' of al-Bahrayn in the dhimma settlement (Ibn Sa'd); Morony (1984).

nodes.label: The bishoprics of Beth Qatraye
nodes.full: From at least 410, the Church of the East organised the Gulf as the province of Beth Qatraye, with bishops on Bahrain, at Tarut, in the al-Hasa oasis, on the Trucial coast (Hatta) and in Oman (Mazun). Christianity was the majority faith of the settled Gulf population through the Sasanian centuries.
nodes.src: Bishops of the Gulf sees in the acts of the Synods of 410, 424, 544, 576, 676 (Synodicon Orientale); the term 'Nestorian' is an external label the church itself did not use.

nodes.label: The Gulf monasteries — Sir Bani Yas, Al-Qusur, Kharg
nodes.full: A string of courtyard monasteries with plastered churches, monks' cells and moulded crosses was founded down the Gulf islands from the mid-6th century. The Sir Bani Yas monastery, established around 600, is the best preserved; the network was still growing on the eve of Islam.
nodes.src: Sir Bani Yas monastery (King & Hellyer; Abu Dhabi DCT); Al-Qusur on Failaka (French/Kuwaiti mission); Kharg island churches; Marawah church.

nodes.label: Jewish communities of eastern Arabia and Oman
nodes.full: Jewish groups lived in the al-Hasa oasis and in Oman through the Sasanian and early Islamic periods, named among the protected communities of the region and remembered in local tradition — one strand of the Gulf's pre-Islamic religious plurality.
nodes.src: 'Jews' among the dhimmis of al-Bahrayn in the Prophet's settlement (Ibn Sa'd); references to Jewish communities in Oman in the Arabic sources (al-Baladhuri).

nodes.label: The plaster crosses of Sir Bani Yas
nodes.full: The Sir Bani Yas church was decorated with moulded gypsum panels — crosses on stepped bases, vine scrolls, rosettes — in a style shared with Church-of-the-East sites in Iraq. It is the finest late-antique Christian art surviving in the Gulf.
nodes.src: Sir Bani Yas stucco corpus (Abu Dhabi DCT; King, 'A Nestorian monastic settlement on the island of Sir Bani Yas', BSOAS 60, 1997).

nodes.label: Courtyard-monastery and church plans
nodes.full: The Gulf monasteries share a plan: a single-aisle church with a raised sanctuary, ranged around a courtyard with cells, a refectory and cisterns. The uniformity shows a connected monastic movement working to a common template.
nodes.src: Comparative plans in Carter, 'Christianity in the Gulf during the first centuries of Islam', AAE 19 (2008).

nodes.label: The Sasanian torpedo jar
nodes.full: Tall, pointed, bitumen-lined storage jars — 'torpedo jars' — are the signature container of the Sasanian and early Islamic Gulf, carrying dates, wine and fish sauce. Sherds of them trace Persian Gulf trade all the way to Sri Lanka and China.
nodes.src: Torpedo/'Sasanian-Islamic' jar distribution studies (Kennet, 'Sasanian and Islamic pottery from Ras al-Khaimah', 2004).

nodes.label: The Syriac school comes to the Gulf
nodes.full: By the 6th century the Gulf monasteries ran schools on the model of Nisibis — teaching Syriac grammar, scripture, the Antiochene commentators and the chant. The manuscript culture and curriculum they built is what made the seventh-century flowering of Qatari writers possible.
nodes.src: The School of Nisibis model and its monastic offshoots (Becker, 'Fear of God and the Beginning of Wisdom', 2006); the Gulf monastic schools implied by the later writers (Brock).

nodes.label: Gabriel of Qatar's liturgical commentary
nodes.full: Gabriel of Qatar wrote the earliest full commentary on the Church of the East's daily services, explaining the meaning of every prayer and rite. It is a primary source for how Christians actually worshipped in the late-antique Gulf.
nodes.src: Gabriel of Qatar, 'Commentary on the Liturgical Offices'; S. Brock's edition and studies; Kozah et al. (2014).

nodes.label: Cosmas Indicopleustes on the Persian Christians of the sea
nodes.full: The merchant-monk Cosmas records a bishop 'appointed from Persia' and a full Christian clergy on Sri Lanka, and Persian Christian traders along the whole route. The Gulf church was one node in a Christian network reaching to India and beyond.
nodes.src: Cosmas Indicopleustes, 'Christian Topography' 3.65 and 11; the Persian Church's Indian Ocean extension.

nodes.label: The Persian Gulf as the Sasanian trade artery
nodes.full: While Byzantium's eastern trade ran through the Red Sea, the Sasanian Empire's ran up the Gulf. Persian ships and merchants — many of them Christians of the Church of the East — dominated the sea route to Sri Lanka and reached the ports of south China.
nodes.src: Cosmas Indicopleustes; the Byzantine–Sasanian 'silk war' over trade routes (Procopius); Sasanian pottery and coins along the Indian Ocean rim.

nodes.label: Sohar rises as the gateway to China
nodes.full: Sohar grew in this period into the greatest port of the Omani coast, later remembered by the geographers as 'the hallway of China and the storehouse of the East'. Its rise made the Batinah coast the economic centre of gravity of southern Arabia.
nodes.src: Sohar excavations (Kervran; Whitehouse); the later encomium in al-Muqaddasi and al-Istakhri applied to the port's long-established role.

nodes.label: The pearl fishery under Persian rule
nodes.full: Sasanian and early Islamic sources continue to name the Gulf's pearls as a prime luxury. The industry ran without interruption through the change of empires — the divers and the merchant fleets outlasting every state that claimed to govern them.
nodes.src: Pearls of al-Bahrayn in the early Arabic geographers (al-Baladhuri; later al-Masudi); continuity of the fishery across the Sasanian–Islamic transition.

nodes.label: Persian oasis development in al-Hasa
nodes.full: The Sasanians invested in the al-Hasa oasis — its springs, canals and date gardens — settling deportees and colonists to farm it. It became the agricultural anchor of the eastern Arabian province and stayed the region's breadbasket for centuries.
nodes.src: al-Tabari on Shapur II's development and settlement of Hajar; the long agricultural importance of al-Hasa.

nodes.label: Julfar and the northern Oman coast
nodes.full: The town at Kush near Julfar shows continuous occupation from the Sasanian into the Islamic period as a minor port and pearling base — the ancestor of the Julfar that would dominate the lower Gulf a thousand years later.
nodes.src: D. Kennet, 'Sasanian and Islamic Pottery from Ras al-Khaimah' (2004), the Kush sequence.

nodes.label: Sasanian deep-water shipping
nodes.full: Persian shipwrights built the sewn-plank vessels that carried Gulf trade to Sri Lanka and China on the monsoon. The technology — no iron nails, hulls stitched with coir and sealed with bitumen and fish oil — remained the Gulf standard into the 20th century.
nodes.src: Descriptions in the later Arabic nautical literature reflecting Sasanian practice; the sewn-boat tradition (Agius, 'Classic Ships of Islam', 2008).

nodes.label: Monastic water systems on the islands
nodes.full: The island monasteries survived on carefully built cisterns, wells and rainwater channels — the same problem the Neolithic islanders had faced, solved with late-antique engineering. Water management was the precondition for a contemplative life on a desert island.
nodes.src: Water installations at Sir Bani Yas and Al-Qusur (excavation reports; Carter 2008).

nodes.label: The aflaj maintained through the imperial changes
nodes.full: The Iron Age falaj systems of Oman kept flowing through Sasanian and early Islamic rule, their upkeep organised by the oasis communities regardless of who governed the coast. Continuity of the water infrastructure meant continuity of settlement.
nodes.src: Long-term falaj continuity in Oman (Wilkinson, 'Water and Tribal Settlement in South-East Arabia', 1977).

nodes.label: The Church of the East as an Indian Ocean network
nodes.full: Beth Qatraye's bishops travelled to synods in Iraq; its monks and traders carried the faith to the Malabar coast, Socotra and Sri Lanka. The Gulf was a link in a Christian chain that stretched, along the trade routes, from Syria to south China.
nodes.src: Synodicon Orientale (Gulf bishops at Iraqi synods); Cosmas Indicopleustes on Christians in India and Ceylon; the Church of the East's Asian mission.

nodes.label: The Prophet's envoys reach the Gulf
nodes.full: Letters and envoys from Medina to al-Mundhir ibn Sawa in Bahrain and the Julanda brothers in Oman brought both regions into Islam by negotiation. The Gulf's entry into the new order was diplomatic before it was military.
nodes.src: The Prophet's letters preserved in the sira and hadith literature (Ibn Sa'd; al-Baladhuri).

nodes.label: Byzantium and Persia divide the Indian Ocean trade
nodes.full: The long Byzantine–Sasanian rivalry had a maritime dimension: Byzantium worked the Red Sea and courted Ethiopia and Yemen, while Persia held the Gulf. Eastern Arabia's prosperity depended on the Gulf route staying the winning one.
nodes.src: Procopius, 'Wars' 1.19–20 on the trade contest; the Aksumite–Himyarite wars as a proxy struggle.

nodes.label: The Sasanians conquer Yemen
nodes.full: Khosrow I sent a force that overthrew the Ethiopian regime in Yemen and made it a Persian province. For a few decades Persia controlled both ends of Arabia — the Gulf and the Bab al-Mandab — and the whole peninsula's trade.
nodes.src: al-Tabari on the Persian conquest of Yemen and the governorship of Wahriz; the Abna as the resulting Persian-Yemeni community.

nodes.label: The empires exhaust themselves
nodes.full: The last Roman–Persian war drained both empires of men and money just as a new religious and political movement was forming in the Hijaz. The Sasanian collapse that followed was not inevitable in 600 — but by 630 the state that had held the Gulf for four centuries had almost nothing left to defend it with.
nodes.src: Howard-Johnston, 'The Last Great War of Antiquity' (2021); the structural weakness of the post-628 Sasanian state.

nodes.label: The deportee and the colonist
nodes.full: Shapur II's settlement of the eastern Arabian oases moved people in both directions — Arab tribes deported into Iran, Persian cavalry colonists and their households planted on the coast. For those uprooted, the making of the Sasanian frontier province was a forced migration.
nodes.src: al-Tabari on Shapur II's deportations and the settlement of Persians (the later Asawira); Morony, 'Iraq after the Muslim Conquest' (1984).

nodes.label: The daughters of the covenant
nodes.full: The Church of the East had an order of consecrated women, the bnāt qyāmā ('daughters of the covenant'), who lived celibate lives of service attached to a church or community. Their presence in the Gulf — later regulated by the 676 synod — gave women a recognised religious role outside marriage and the household.
nodes.src: The bnāt/bnay qyāmā institution in the Church of the East (Harvey; Brock); the regulation of consecrated women in the later Synod of Dayrin canons.
